subtitle: Compare the medical, social and rights-based models of disability to understand how health, social barriers and rights each shape the questions we ask about disability.
scope: For staff across DHS, including staff in clinical roles. This course introduces ways of understanding disability; it does not assess a person, prescribe treatment, decide eligibility or replace an applicable legal or accommodation process. Use practice cases or private, unrecorded reflection. Personal health information and a live work product are not required. Native American- and Tribal-specific matters are referred to the appropriate office within ADSA.
introTranscript: A person may seek treatment for pain, ask for a usable communication method and want a voice in a decision that affects their life. Those needs are connected, but they are not the same question. Medical, social and rights-based models of disability highlight different parts of the picture. Learning these perspectives can help you notice when one explanation leaves something important out. Clinical care can be valuable without becoming the only account of a person. Removing a barrier can support participation without making a health need unreal. A rights-based approach asks how people’s dignity, agency and equal participation are respected, while actual duties still follow the applicable law and policy. We will compare the perspectives through practice DHS situations, then practice choosing questions that fit the issue. You can reflect privately at your own pace; no disability disclosure or personal assessment is part of this course.

intro.heading: Notice what an explanation places at the center
intro.body:
Consider a practice service-orientation session. Sasha asks for a way to follow the discussion because rapid spoken instructions are difficult to hear. Sasha also has a separate health concern being discussed with an appropriate clinician. Staff can respond to these circumstances in different ways. One explanation asks what treatment might improve hearing. Another asks why the session depends on rapid speech alone. A third asks how Sasha can receive information and participate as an equal person with a say in the approach.

Medical, social and rights-based perspectives help distinguish those questions. A medical model focuses on a condition or impairment and individual treatment or adjustment. A social model places attention on barriers in the physical, social and organizational environment. A rights-based perspective emphasizes dignity, agency, non-discrimination and participation rather than making a person’s value depend on becoming more like a presumed norm. These are broad ways of understanding an issue, not complete accounts of every person or setting.

The distinction matters because a reasonable question can become too narrow. Treatment may be useful for Sasha’s health goal, but a possible future improvement does not explain how the present orientation will be usable. Changing the format may support participation, but it does not prove that the separate health concern is imaginary. Calling Sasha a rights holder also does not determine every actual service requirement without its applicable law, evidence and process.

The WHO’s ICF discussion brings health and environmental perspectives together rather than reducing disability to one dimension. The UN Committee’s rights-model discussion adds an explicit focus on people as subjects of rights and acknowledges disability among several dimensions of identity. These conceptual sources help compare explanations. They do not give a course participant permission to assess Sasha or decide a legal claim.

You may privately reflect on which question you tend to notice first. That awareness has value without a work metric or a disclosure. You can also stay with the practice session. Do not assign a model to a colleague’s character, infer an intercultural orientation or require anyone to tell a personal health story.

items.title: One question can be useful and incomplete
items.body: A clinician may appropriately explore Sasha’s health concern through the clinical process. That does not answer the format question for the orientation. Recognizing this limit is different from blaming clinical work. Ask which problem the response addresses and what another responsible role still needs to consider.

items.title: A model is not a person’s identity
items.body: People may use several explanations for different purposes. A staff member who asks a health question is not automatically committed to every assumption described as a medical model. Discuss the actual question and consequence rather than assigning a character judgment or a personal developmental label.

items.title: Give separate needs separate attention
items.body: Sasha’s participation concern and health concern can both matter. A format review can proceed within the responsible service process while clinical questions remain with suitable professionals. Do not require one need to disappear before the other is recognized; identify what information and authority each decision needs.

tabs.label: Only a health explanation
tabs.body: The explanation may identify a useful treatment question but leave the session’s communication method unchanged. Sasha could still lack usable information now. The next inquiry is not whether treatment is bad; it is what the orientation process must address while health questions use their proper clinical route.

tabs.label: Only an environmental explanation
tabs.body: The explanation may reveal that the session relies on one method, but can become incomplete if it dismisses Sasha’s own health goal. Removing a barrier does not settle every personal symptom or care need. Keep the format question and the person’s separately expressed health question clear.

tabs.label: Connected questions with agency
tabs.body: The explanation asks about health needs, the environment and Sasha’s role in the decision. Different professionals or processes may address different parts. This approach does not guarantee a specific aid, treatment or benefit; it makes the questions more complete without treating the person as a problem to be solved.

check.question: Which reading best captures the practice orientation issue?
check.correct: Health needs, the session’s communication method and Sasha’s participation can all matter, with different decisions using their appropriate roles and evidence.
wrong: A treatment possibility automatically resolves present participation.
Changing the session proves the health concern is not real.
Mentioning a model diagnoses Sasha or determines every legal entitlement.
check.feedbackCorrect: The reading separates related questions and preserves both the person’s agency and actual decision roles.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Possible treatment does not explain present usability. A barrier change does not erase a health concern, and a conceptual model does not diagnose or establish every legal entitlement. Ask what each explanation addresses and what remains to be considered through the proper process.

What clinical information would a qualified professional need for the actual care decision?

A staff member’s one question reveals their personal developmental orientation.

lessons.transfer: Privately consider which question you notice first, or compare the practice explanations for Sasha. No personal assessment, disclosure or recorded answer is required.

move.control: You can examine the scope and consequences of an explanation.
move.failure: One perspective becomes the entire person, or a conceptual model becomes a diagnosis.
move.next: Name the useful question and the relevant question that remains unanswered.

intro.heading: Understand the medical perspective and its limits
intro.body:
The medical model directs attention to a condition or impairment and the possibilities for individual treatment, rehabilitation or adjustment. It can frame useful clinical questions: what is causing a symptom, what care options are appropriate, and what matters to the person in choosing among them? A qualified professional may need relevant clinical information for an actual care decision. This course does not supply that assessment or authorize a learner to prescribe, diagnose or change someone’s care.

The limit appears when a health explanation becomes the only way to understand participation. Sasha’s hearing-related health question does not reveal every preferred communication method, ability or goal. A diagnosis alone cannot tell staff whether the orientation’s rapid speech is usable. It also does not decide whether another person should speak for Sasha. The actual task, environment and Sasha’s account still need attention.

In another practice case, Maren experiences pain and wants to discuss treatment with a suitable clinician. A colleague says that acknowledging pain gives too much weight to the medical model and urges Maren to focus only on social barriers. That dismisses a health concern Maren has actually expressed. Another colleague says the diagnosis explains everything and assumes Maren cannot contribute to a planning discussion. That extends a clinical fact into an unsupported account of participation.

A more careful response allows appropriate care and examines the task separately. What does Maren want from the clinical discussion? What is required to contribute to the planning discussion, and what supports or changes could be relevant? The person’s goals belong in the conversation. Health care and barrier removal do not have to compete as though valuing one requires abandoning the other.

Clinical work also has its own consent, privacy and professional responsibilities. An ordinary coworker or supervisor does not gain clinical authority from learning these models. In state-employment accommodation, Policy 1433 gives medical-documentation roles to the ADA Coordinator, not supervisors or managers, and agencies do not request or accept medical records as accommodation documentation. Keep that distinct from an authorized clinical-care relationship. You may learn through Maren’s practice example without using or sharing anyone’s health information.

What the person wants to address, such as a health concern, participation task or both; not a preference invented from a diagnosis.
Clinical-care and employment-accommodation processes have different purposes and responsibilities. A course does not merge or transfer them.

items.title: Do not dismiss wanted care
items.body: Maren’s wish to discuss pain is not a rejection of accessibility or equality. A social explanation can illuminate barriers without telling Maren that the health concern is invalid. Respect the expressed goal and the appropriate care process, while remaining attentive to the separate participation question.

items.title: Do not extend a health label into a whole-life conclusion
items.body: A diagnosis may be relevant to a qualified care decision but does not automatically decide which tasks a person can perform, what they prefer or who should speak for them. In the practice planning discussion, ask about the relevant contribution and support instead of substituting an assumed limitation.

items.title: Keep the role of the information clear
items.body: A clinical professional may have a legitimate care-related information need. A supervisor evaluating an employment-accommodation request has a different role under Policy 1433 and must not request medical information or documentation. The topic is not a general ban on clinical records in authorized care; it is a reason to preserve each process’s actual authority and privacy.

tabs.label: Diagnosis as the complete explanation
tabs.body: This approach may acknowledge a health condition but treat it as enough to decide participation, preference and support. It bypasses the person’s account and the task’s actual demands. A clinical fact should inform the question for which it is relevant, without becoming an unsupported explanation for everything else.

tabs.label: Care dismissed as the wrong perspective
tabs.body: This approach notices social barriers but denies the value of a health concern the person wants addressed. It turns a conceptual distinction into pressure about which needs count. Respect appropriate care and ask what other environmental or participation questions still need attention.

tabs.label: Care with scope and participation
tabs.body: This approach values a clinical question within the authorized care process and separately examines participation with the person. It recognizes that different information and decision roles may apply. It neither promises a treatment outcome nor transfers clinical or accommodation authority to someone who lacks it.

check.question: Which response best respects Maren’s expressed health concern and participation?
check.correct: Allow the care question to use its appropriate clinical process and examine the planning task with Maren, without inferring ability or preference from a diagnosis.
wrong: Tell Maren that wanting pain treatment is incompatible with a social view of disability.
Assume the diagnosis means Maren cannot contribute.
Ask a supervisor to collect medical records as employment-accommodation documentation.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response preserves the person’s goals, clinical scope and the separate participation question.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Wanting care does not invalidate concern about barriers. A diagnosis does not determine every contribution or preference. Policy 1433 prohibits supervisor or manager medical-information requests, and agencies do not request or accept medical records as accommodation documentation. Use the responsible process rather than merging clinical care and employment roles.

items.text: Maren wants to discuss a symptom with a suitable clinician.
An authorized clinical-care decision uses its applicable consent, privacy and professional requirements.
What does the planning task require, and what contribution does Maren want to make?
Which environmental supports could be relevant to the task?
A diagnosis automatically makes another person the speaker for Maren.
A manager requests medical records for an employment-accommodation decision.

move.failure: Care is dismissed, or a diagnosis becomes an automatic judgment about the whole person.

lessons.title: Understand social barriers and the environment
lessons.summary: Examine how a method, setting or expectation can restrict participation without dismissing health needs.
lessons.objective: Identify physical, communication and organizational barriers in a practice participation task.
objectives: Identify physical, communication and organizational barriers in a practice participation task.
Distinguish an environmental explanation from an unsupported claim that every impairment disappears when a barrier changes.
Choose a task-focused inquiry that includes the person’s account and avoids diagnosing the cause of every difficulty.
takeaways: Participation depends partly on the environment and how activities are organized.
A common method is not automatically usable by everyone.
Barrier removal and appropriate personal support can work together.
lessons.statement: Examine the task and environment before locating every difficulty inside the person.

image.caption: A facilitator writes on a whiteboard while a group follows along at a long table.

intro.heading: Understand social barriers and the environment
intro.body:
A social model asks how the surroundings and organization of an activity contribute to disability-related exclusion. The environment includes more than the building. It can include how information is presented, which communication methods count, whether a person can influence a decision, and the assumptions behind a rule. The perspective directs attention toward changes in the shared setting rather than making every difficulty a personal deficit to correct.

Return to Sasha’s practice service orientation. The facilitator presents a sequence of instructions rapidly, with no usable way to revisit the information. Telling Sasha to listen harder does not examine that format. An environmental inquiry asks what must be communicated, how the information is delivered and what appropriate methods would support the actual task. It does not begin by judging Sasha’s effort or treating one format as evidence of the ability to understand.

A useful inquiry also remains specific. Staff should not assume that all people with hearing-related disabilities use sign language, prefer written text or need the same aid. DOJ’s effective-communication guidance connects the task’s nature and complexity with the individual’s communication methods. A change useful in one conversation may not be enough in another. In the practice case, staff need the person’s account and appropriate service guidance, rather than choosing an aid solely from a diagnosis.

The social perspective can become too narrow if it treats health needs as irrelevant or assumes that changing one feature removes every limitation. Maren’s pain concern remains a legitimate question for appropriate care even if a meeting method changes. The WHO’s ICF explanation connects health and contextual factors; it does not require choosing between them as mutually exclusive truths.

For a practice activity, identify the specific feature and the task it affects. Ask what the person wants to accomplish and which appropriate review or support process can address it. Do not turn a practice suggestion into a universal design rule or a legal finding. You may privately notice which routines you have assumed were neutral, without recording a personal story or requiring someone else to disclose a disability.

flashcards.back: A feature of the physical, social or organizational setting that can restrict a particular participation task.
A relevant feature or support that helps make a task possible; effectiveness still needs attention.
A question about what the person needs to receive, convey or do in the actual situation, rather than an assumed deficit.
People with the same diagnostic description may use different methods or have different goals; do not select every response from the label.

items.title: Look beyond the building
items.body: A room may be physically accessible while the way a discussion is organized makes a contribution difficult. In Sasha’s orientation, the issue includes the pace and communication method. Examining those features broadens the inquiry without establishing that every feature is unlawful or that a single change resolves all needs.

items.title: A familiar method is still a choice
items.body: Rapid spoken instruction may feel ordinary to the facilitator, but familiarity does not demonstrate that it is effective for the particular task and person. Ask what information must be received and conveyed. A suitable service review can consider alternatives without making a person’s method an unnecessary test of effort or intelligence.

items.title: Check what the change addresses
items.body: A revised information format may help Sasha follow the orientation. That does not show that separate symptoms, care needs or every future task are resolved. Identify the intended task and examine effectiveness there. Keeping the scope clear helps staff avoid both dismissing useful improvements and overstating what they prove.

tabs.label: The person must fit the existing method
tabs.body: This approach assumes that the activity’s familiar format is fixed and that difficulty belongs only to the person. It can miss a barrier created by how the task is organized. Examine the feature and actual requirement before asking the person to compensate for it; do not infer effort or ability from one method.

tabs.label: One change fixes every need
tabs.body: This approach recognizes an environmental feature but turns a useful response into a complete explanation of the person’s life. A usable orientation format does not determine a separate health goal or every later communication task. Keep improvements specific and check their effectiveness rather than declaring disability erased.

tabs.label: Person, task and environment considered together
tabs.body: This approach asks what Sasha needs to accomplish, how the session is organized and which appropriate support or change can help. It preserves health questions and actual service requirements. A proposed change still needs the responsible process and evidence; the conceptual explanation is a starting point for inquiry.

check.question: Which inquiry best uses a social perspective in Sasha’s practice orientation?
check.correct: Examine the rapid spoken format and actual communication task, include Sasha’s account and use the appropriate process to consider effective methods.
wrong: Infer low effort because Sasha cannot use the familiar method.
Choose sign language automatically for everyone with hearing-related disability.
Claim that one format change removes every health need and participation limitation.
check.feedbackCorrect: The inquiry makes the environmental feature visible while retaining the person’s methods and the actual task.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A method difficulty does not prove low effort. Diagnostic descriptions do not determine everyone’s communication method. A useful environmental change also does not erase all health needs or establish future effectiveness. Ask about the task and person, then examine suitable responses through the appropriate process.

sorting.heading: Distinguish useful questions and unsupported assumptions

items.text: The instructions are available only as rapid speech.
The activity allows only one way to contribute.
What information must Sasha receive and convey?
Which methods are effective for this person and communication task?
Difficulty with one method proves lack of effort.
Changing one format makes every health need irrelevant.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: A facilitator says Sasha must adapt to the usual spoken orientation because that is how the session has always worked.
scenario.prompt: Which response best examines the environmental question?
options: Treat the familiar format as proof that every participant should be able to use it.
Ask about the communication task, Sasha’s methods and the available appropriate service response without inferring effort or denying health needs.
Assume one generic aid will work for every hearing-related disability.
responses: Familiarity is not evidence of effectiveness for this person and task.
This makes the feature and the person’s account visible while retaining actual responsibilities.
The diagnostic category does not select an effective method for everyone.

lessons.transfer: Use the practice orientation to identify a feature, a task and a question about participation, or reflect privately on a routine you have treated as neutral. No disclosure or live investigation is required.

move.control: You can identify an environmental contribution to a participation difficulty.
move.failure: A familiar method becomes a test of the person, or one changed feature becomes proof that every need is resolved.
move.next: Ask what the task requires and how the environment affects the person’s opportunity to participate.

lessons.title: Understand a rights-based perspective
lessons.summary: Recognize dignity, agency and equal participation while keeping actual legal duties and decisions clear.
lessons.objective: Explain how a rights-based perspective treats people as participants and rights holders rather than objects of care.
objectives: Explain how a rights-based perspective treats people as participants and rights holders rather than objects of care.
Distinguish a conceptual human-rights explanation from the applicable U.S. law or DHS policy for an actual decision.

takeaways: A person’s dignity and agency do not depend on curing an impairment.

image.caption: A facilitator writes on a whiteboard while a group follows along at a long table.

intro.heading: Understand a rights-based perspective
intro.body:
A rights-based perspective asks whether people are treated as subjects of rights and participants in decisions, rather than simply as recipients of treatment or help. It emphasizes dignity, non-discrimination, equality and agency. The UN Committee’s discussion of the human-rights model recognizes disability as one dimension of a person’s identity, not a reason to reduce them to an impairment. Its account is an international conceptual source; it does not itself establish every DHS legal obligation.

Actual U.S. duties require their applicable law and policy. ADA Title II addresses state and local government programs and activities, with qualified requirements for participation, reasonable modifications and effective communication. The relevant rules and authorized process determine how a particular issue is addressed. Calling an approach rights-based does not create eligibility for any requested service, authorize staff to ignore another requirement or decide a legal dispute from a course exercise.

In a practice service-planning discussion, staff plan to explain Sasha’s options to a companion while Sasha is present. They assume it will be easier because Sasha has difficulty with the spoken format. A rights-based question asks how Sasha can receive information, convey preferences and take part with appropriate communication support. Difficulty with one method does not automatically transfer all decisions to someone else. Actual representation arrangements and privacy requirements still matter, and this lesson does not cancel them.

This perspective also changes how help is understood. Providing an aid as a favor makes the opportunity seem dependent on staff generosity. Examining the applicable duty treats access as a responsibility where the requirements apply. At the same time, the particular aid must be effective for the task and person. For Title II communication, primary consideration of the person’s request has the rule’s actual context and legal limits; it is neither staff convenience alone nor an unlimited promise of every preferred method.

You may reflect privately on whether your picture of good service includes agency as well as assistance. Use Sasha’s invented discussion if you prefer. No learner needs to prove a personal commitment, disclose a health condition or adjudicate an actual rights claim. Thoughtful understanding and the real decision process remain connected but distinct.

flashcards.back: A person with dignity and applicable rights, rather than a passive object of treatment or charity.
The person’s opportunity to express views, preferences and choices within the actual decision context.
An obligation from the law or policy that covers the actual setting, with its qualifications and responsible roles.
An explanation that helps frame understanding; it is not automatically a directly applicable rule for every DHS case.

items.title: Assistance does not erase participation
items.body: Sasha may use communication assistance and still have preferences and relevant knowledge. Staff should examine an appropriate route for the person’s contribution instead of automatically replacing it with a companion’s presumed account. Actual authority and representation arrangements remain in force; a course cannot invent or remove them.

items.title: Distinguish a favor from a responsibility
items.body: A warm offer may be welcome, but staff generosity is not the basis of an applicable access duty. When the actual requirement applies, use the responsible process to provide effective participation rather than treating access as a reward for gratitude. Do not infer a legal finding from a practice example or declare every request automatically required.

items.title: Identify the actual authority
items.body: The UN conceptual discussion, a U.S. regulation and a DHS policy serve different purposes. Do not cite an international model as though it supplies a particular DHS eligibility criterion. In a real question, identify the covered setting, applicable requirement and responsible decision maker, then seek appropriate guidance where needed.

tabs.label: Care without a role for the person
tabs.body: This approach may provide help but leave the person’s preferences and contribution out of the decision. In Sasha’s practice discussion, convenience could become substitution. Appropriate support should help participation without assuming that a communication difficulty transfers decision authority to another person.

tabs.label: A rights label promises every outcome
tabs.body: This approach recognizes dignity but skips the actual requirement, evidence and authorized decision. It can turn an important principle into a promise staff cannot make. Use the applicable law and policy, including their qualifications, while retaining the person’s opportunity to participate in the process.

tabs.label: Agency with actual responsibilities
tabs.body: This approach includes Sasha’s account through effective communication and identifies the actual decision roles. It values dignity while preserving privacy, representation and applicable requirements. The course can teach the distinction without deciding what particular service or legal remedy a real person must receive.

check.question: Which approach best uses a rights-based perspective in the practice planning discussion?
check.correct: Provide an appropriate route for Sasha’s information and contribution while preserving actual representation, privacy and applicable service requirements.
wrong: Speak only to the companion because a communication difficulty transfers every decision.
Promise any requested service because a conceptual model is enough to establish eligibility.
Treat required access as a favor that depends on gratitude.
check.feedbackCorrect: The approach values agency and uses the actual responsibilities for the setting rather than replacing them with assumptions.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A communication difficulty does not automatically transfer authority. A conceptual model does not determine eligibility or every requested service. Where an access duty applies, gratitude is not its basis. Include the person and use the applicable process without inventing authority or a legal finding.

intro.heading: Compare the perspectives through one situation
intro.body:
In a practice DHS advisory activity, Jules wants to contribute to a discussion about a service proposal. Jules has an ongoing pain concern being addressed through appropriate care and asks about a way to participate without a long uninterrupted session. The organizer must consider the activity’s actual purpose and requirements. The learning case does not supply a medical assessment, decide a legal accommodation or establish every possible arrangement.

A health-focused question asks what Jules wants to address with the appropriate care professional. It does not authorize the organizer to recommend medication or collect a diagnosis. An environmental question examines the session structure and the contribution task: what information is needed, when discussion occurs and whether suitable ways of contributing could reduce the particular barrier. A rights-based question asks how Jules’s views and applicable participation needs are considered, with actual responsibilities and decision roles intact.

Compare three proposed responses. One organizer tells Jules to return after treatment improves the pain, leaving the present task unexamined. Another says that changing the session makes care unnecessary, dismissing a separate goal Jules has expressed. A third asks about the contribution Jules wants to make and the relevant task, while coordinating the request through the proper process and leaving clinical questions with suitable professionals. The third approach is more complete because it distinguishes the questions, not because it guarantees one arrangement or proves the other staff have bad motives.

Evidence still matters. The fact that a proposed method exists does not show that it works for Jules or that every participant has the same need. A useful review asks what the response is intended to enable, what the person reports and what the actual process must examine. Do not infer a population rate, symptom cause or legal violation from the practice account. Participation can be assessed for its particular purpose without judging Jules’s worth or gratitude.

You can practice with the invented situation or reflect privately on why you tend to prefer one kind of explanation. Recognizing an assumption is useful personal learning even if no work document results. A real request or clinical duty still follows its applicable process; completing this comparison does not replace it.

Compare responses by what they address and leave unanswered rather than ranking the person or profession.
Identify evidence, authority and a next step needed before a proposed response becomes an actual decision.
Which response is more complete?
lessons.keyStatement: Compare what each response accomplishes, and keep the person’s goals in view.

flashcards.back: What does Jules want to address through appropriate care? The organizer does not prescribe or assess from the course.
How does the session structure affect the actual contribution task, and which suitable alternatives merit review?
How will Jules’s agency and applicable participation needs inform the responsible decision process?
Examine what each option addresses, leaves unknown and requires before action; it is not a score of a person or a profession.

items.title: Ask about the contribution, not a presumed deficit
items.body: Jules wants to address a service proposal. The organizer can clarify the relevant task and requested participation change without inventing a symptom cause or recommending treatment. Knowing what the activity requires makes the environmental question more precise and leaves clinical questions where they belong.

items.title: A fuller inquiry is not a guaranteed approval
items.body: The connected response still needs the actual process, relevant evidence and authority. It cannot promise a particular arrangement simply because three perspectives were considered. The advantage is a better account of the questions and responsibilities, including the person’s own goals and the unknowns.

items.title: Compare consequences without diagnosing motives
items.body: The treatment-first response leaves the current task unanswered; the barrier-only response dismisses a health goal. Those consequences can be explained without labeling the organizers as uncaring or assigning an intercultural stage. Focus on the proposed action and what it would or would not address.

tabs.label: Wait for treatment to solve participation
tabs.body: This response places the present opportunity behind a hoped-for clinical change. It does not examine the activity’s structure or the requested support. Appropriate care may matter, but the organizer cannot presume its result or use that possibility as the entire answer to a present participation question.

tabs.label: Change the activity and dismiss care
tabs.body: This response notices the environment but tells Jules what health needs should matter. It overstates what a task change can establish and disregards a separately expressed goal. A useful improvement does not require the person to abandon appropriate care or agree that symptoms are no longer important.

tabs.label: Coordinate the questions and preserve the person’s goals
tabs.body: This response asks about the contribution task, the requested change and the responsible process, while keeping care with appropriate professionals. It values agency and evidence without guaranteeing an outcome. It also leaves room for further inquiry if the proposed method does not enable the intended participation.

check.question: What makes the connected response to Jules more complete?
check.correct: It distinguishes the health goal, activity structure and participation responsibilities, includes Jules’s account and identifies what the actual process must still examine.
wrong: It proves that every proposed adjustment must be approved.
It shows that care becomes unnecessary after any environmental change.
It diagnoses the organizers’ values and personal developmental positions.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response makes relevant questions visible while preserving evidence, authority and the person’s goals.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Considering several perspectives does not automatically approve a method or resolve a health concern. The comparison examines proposed actions, not people’s character or developmental positions. Keep the task, person’s account, unknowns and actual process clear before making a real decision.

sorting.heading: Distinguish useful questions and unsupported assumptions

items.text: Which part of Jules’s goal does each response address?
What remains unanswered about the contribution task and the person’s needs?
Clinical questions remain with suitable professionals.
The responsible process examines a real participation request.
A three-perspective comparison automatically authorizes every adjustment.
The response identifies a staff member’s personal developmental orientation.

options: Assume treatment will resolve every contribution barrier.
Dismiss the expressed care goal because only the activity’s structure matters.

responses: The organizer cannot presume that clinical result or leave the present task unexamined.
Environmental inquiry does not erase the person’s health goal.
This separates connected questions and preserves evidence and authority without promising a result.

lessons.transfer: Use the practice options to compare what each response addresses and leaves unknown, or reflect privately on an assumption you recognize. No health disclosure, live case or personal assessment is required.

move.control: You can compare the scope and consequences of different responses.
move.failure: Care, environment and agency become rival choices, or a fuller inquiry is mistaken for automatic approval.
move.next: Keep the expressed goals, task, evidence and responsible next step connected.

intro.heading: Carry the understanding into learning and practice
intro.body:
Learning these perspectives is not a test of which model you can attach to a person. The useful change is in the questions you can now recognize. A clinical explanation may address an expressed health goal. A social explanation can reveal how a method or expectation creates a barrier. A rights-based explanation keeps dignity, agency and applicable responsibilities visible. The perspectives can inform each other while retaining differences in purpose and authority.

Return to Sasha’s orientation and Jules’s advisory activity. You do not need to decide a diagnosis, an entitlement or an actual legal claim to describe what was missing from a narrow response. You can identify the communication or contribution task, the person’s expressed question and what the responsible process still needs to examine. The cases show why neither hoped-for treatment nor a generic barrier change can serve as a complete answer to every need.

Personal understanding is also part of the learning. You may notice that your idea of helping has been shaped by solving an individual problem, changing a shared environment or defending a right. That reflection can deepen how you understand agency and support. It does not have to become a recorded answer, a public statement or a measurable work outcome. No colleague needs to provide a disability or care history as material for your insight.

When an actual question arises, use its current process. A clinical decision needs suitable clinical authority and evidence. An employment-accommodation request uses Policy 1433 and actual agency roles, including the prohibition on supervisor or manager medical-information requests. A public-service communication issue uses the applicable requirements and responsible service response. A relevant policy review still follows DHS’s required equity work. Optional course completion does not substitute for any of these duties or authorize a decision outside the role.

For the final activity, choose a practice case or a suitable authorized draft without personal information. State the useful health question, environmental question and agency or duty question. Then identify what remains unknown and which responsible role or process would address it. You can also finish through private reflection alone. The purpose is thoughtful understanding and clearer inquiry, without making the course a personal assessment or a certification of actual compliance.

lessons.keyStatement: Carry a clearer question forward rather than claiming that learning has settled the whole issue.

flashcards.back: An explanation that recognizes relevant health, environmental and agency questions without reducing the person to one dimension.
Personal inquiry that can remain unrecorded and unshared; it is not personnel evidence or an access gate.
A question tied to the actual task, person’s account and unknowns, rather than a claim that the whole issue is settled.
A duty and decision role from the applicable process, which optional learning does not replace or expand.

items.title: Recognize insight without requiring performance
items.body: A learner may better understand why assistance should preserve a person’s agency before any work outcome changes. That is meaningful learning. Do not demand a private story, proof of a belief change or a completed live case to make it count. Actual work responsibilities still need their own action and evidence.

items.title: Use the model to improve the question
items.body: A draft may call a participation difficulty an individual limitation. Ask which task is involved and whether the environment or decision approach also needs attention. Do not automatically replace the sentence with a legal finding or assume the opposite cause. The conceptual comparison helps clarify what appropriate inquiry is needed.

items.title: Check effectiveness without making it a person’s score
items.body: A proposed communication method can be reviewed for whether it supports the intended task. That does not rate the person’s dignity, gratitude or personal development. Keep evidence tied to the actual purpose and privacy requirements. One successful exchange also does not prove that the method will work for every task or person.

tabs.label: A single correct label for every person
tabs.body: This approach turns a conceptual comparison into a classification of individuals. It loses the different purposes of care, barrier inquiry and rights questions. Use the perspectives to examine an explanation or proposed response, not to attach a model, orientation or belief score to a colleague.

tabs.label: Learning as proof that duties are complete
tabs.body: This approach confuses understanding with actual authority and performance. Completing a reflection does not provide a service, assess a condition or complete required policy analysis. It can improve the questions you bring to the real process while preserving the work that the applicable requirements still demand.

tabs.label: Understanding with bounded next steps
tabs.body: This approach values private insight and clearer inquiry, then identifies the actual process when work is needed. It does not require a live case to complete learning or make a compliance claim. A practical next question can remain practice while a real request follows its responsible roles and requirements.

check.question: Which final activity fits the purpose of this course?
check.correct: Use a practice case, suitable authorized draft or private reflection to distinguish relevant questions and identify what an actual decision would still need, without claiming a personal assessment or compliance.
wrong: Assign a medical or social model to each colleague’s character.
Require everyone to share a health history before completing the course.
Treat a reflection as proof that clinical, service and policy duties are finished.
check.feedbackCorrect: The activity values understanding and a clearer question while preserving privacy and actual decision responsibilities.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The models are not labels for colleagues or diagnoses of their character. Personal health disclosure is not required. Learning also does not perform a clinical assessment, provide a service or complete mandatory analysis. Keep the exercise private or practice as appropriate, and use the real process for actual duties.

sorting.heading: Distinguish useful questions and unsupported assumptions

items.text: Privately examine which explanation you notice first.
Compare the questions left unanswered in a practice response.
A real clinical decision uses suitable authority and evidence.
A relevant policy review still uses the required equity process.
Every learner must disclose a disability or health history.
Reflection certifies that every service and accommodation duty is complete.

lessons.next: Continue at your own pace: Use the job aid to keep the questions and responsibilities clear

scenario.context: Practice DHS learning case: You have compared Sasha’s orientation options. No clinical assessment, service determination or legal review has occurred.
options: The exercise completed every actual duty associated with the orientation.
You can identify fuller questions about health, format and participation, while actual decisions still need their responsible process and evidence.
Everyone with Sasha’s diagnostic description must use the same aid.
responses: A learning exercise is not performance or certification of actual duties.
This recognizes learning without inventing an assessment, finding or finished outcome.
The diagnosis does not determine the method for every person and task.

lessons.transfer: Finish with private reflection, a practice case or a suitable authorized draft. Identify a useful question and what an actual decision would still require. No disclosure or live work product is required.

move.control: You can learn privately and ask fuller, task-specific questions when appropriate.
move.failure: A model becomes a personal label, disclosure becomes a learning gate, or reflection becomes automatic compliance.
move.next: Preserve the person’s agency and use the applicable evidence and process for actual work.

jobAid.subtitle: Compare perspectives without reducing the person to one explanation.
remember: A health question, an environmental barrier and a participation right can all be relevant.
Appropriate care does not resolve every environmental question; barrier removal does not make a health concern unreal.
Diagnosis does not determine every ability, preference or communication method.
A conceptual model does not authorize clinical, eligibility, service or legal decisions.
Private understanding has value without disclosure, a personal score or a live work-product requirement.

sections.heading: Ask what the explanation emphasizes
items: Medical: What health goal does the person want addressed through suitable care?
Social: How does the physical, communication or organizational environment affect the actual task?
Rights-based: How are dignity, agency, participation and applicable responsibilities considered?
What does the explanation leave unanswered, and what relevant evidence is still needed?

sections.heading: Compare responses by their purpose and limits
items: Does the response address the person’s expressed goal, or assume a preference from a diagnosis?
Does a hoped-for treatment result leave a present participation question unanswered?
Does a proposed environmental change dismiss a separate health concern or overstate its effectiveness?
Does the rights explanation identify actual requirements and decision roles rather than promise every outcome?

sections.heading: Keep learning and actual decisions clear
items: Use practice cases or private, unrecorded reflection. No disability or health disclosure is required.
Clinical decisions remain with suitable professionals and the applicable care process.

In state-employment accommodation, supervisors and managers do not request medical information or documentation. Appropriate requests belong to the ADA Coordinator; medical records are not accepted as accommodation documentation.
Public-service participation and policy questions still use their applicable requirements, evidence and responsible roles. Optional learning does not replace required action.

sources.title: WHO: ICF beginner’s guide
sources.note: Conceptual discussion of medical and social models and their integration in ICF, with functioning and environmental context. This historical explanation is not a DHS eligibility rule or clinical protocol.

sources.title: UN Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities: General Comment No. 6
sources.note: Paragraphs 8–11 explain the human-rights model and inclusive equality. The comment addresses the Convention’s States parties; this course uses the conceptual discussion without presenting it as a directly applicable DHS legal rule.

sources.title: DOJ: Guide to disability rights laws
sources.note: Distinguishes actual U.S. coverage questions, including ADA Title II and Section 504. A conceptual perspective is not a substitute for the applicable requirements.

sources.title: DOJ: Effective communication
sources.note: Explains the nature, length, complexity and context of communication and the person’s usual methods. Title II primary consideration has actual effectiveness and legal limits; neither a diagnosis nor staff convenience selects every aid.

sources.title: 28 CFR 35.130: General prohibitions against discrimination
sources.note: Current Title II rule for public entities. Its qualified duties and exceptions remain actual legal questions; this lesson makes no finding about a live service.

sources.title: 28 CFR 35.160: General communication requirements
sources.note: Current public-entity effective-communication requirements, including primary consideration. The course does not authorize an informal exception or an individual benefit determination.

sources.title: DHS Equity Policy
sources.note: Agency responsibilities for equity in relevant policies and practices. Optional conceptual learning does not replace required tools, analysis or authorized decisions.

sources.title: MMB Policy 1433: Reasonable accommodation
sources.note: Formal state-employment accommodation roles and privacy requirements. Supervisors and managers do not request medical information or documentation; appropriate documentation requests belong to the ADA Coordinator, and agencies do not request or accept medical records.
